archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (possession-first)
archetype.definition: A Montréal team that owns the puck and the chances at 5-on-5 well beyond its .500-ish record and negative goal differential, held back by goaltending and a quiet power play rather than by how it plays.

report.headline: Montréal is driving play like a contender; the crease is hiding it.
report.take:
Eight games in, the Canadiens look like a middling team on the standings page and a good one under the hood. Their 4-3-1 record and a -0.37 Goal Diff / GP (22nd) put them 20th on the site, but their 5-on-5 numbers are among the league's best: a .543 xGF % (7th) and a .55 CF % (6th). That is a sharp break from their history. Even last year's 106-point, nine-playoff-win team posted only a .479 xGF % and won with finishing and goaltending (a 101.8 PDO, 22.4 GSAx). This year the process has caught up, and the results have not.

The gap is the crease. The team save percentage is .868 across all situations, 28th and well under the league's .893, and Goalies GSAx sits at -2.3. Those numbers are really one goalie's. Jacob Fowler has been fine: .900, +2.2 GSAx and a shutout in his four starts. Jakub Dobes has been a problem: .842, a 4.63 GAA and -5.8 GSAx in his four. The result is 3.75 goals allowed a game, 27th, against a team allowing only 25.5 shots a game (12th). The defense is not the leak. The power play is the other drag at 14.8% (25th), well under the league's 20.4%, which is odd for a group with Lane Hutson, Nick Suzuki and Cole Caufield.

The record also flatters the differential a little. Most of the wins have needed overtime, including the 1-0 game against Detroit and both 4-3 wins over Buffalo, and Pts vs Goal Diff is +0.9 (7th). Underneath, though, the scoring line is real. At 3.38 goals a game the offense ranks 9th, and the shot volume backs it up (29.1 a game). Suzuki (10 points, 10th on the centers tab) and Hutson (8 points in 26.5 minutes, 8th among defensemen) are driving it. The depth scoring from Zachary Bolduc and Josh Anderson, four goals each, has also mattered. The weak spots up front are Jake Evans, still without a point, and Alex Newhook's .468 xGF %.

The direction is good. A 96.7 PDO on a team that outshoots and out-chances opponents is the kind of number that climbs. If the goaltending gets even close to league average, this goal differential flips positive. The 92-point pace is a floor more than a ceiling, as long as Fowler keeps taking the starts he has earned.

strengths.title: Controlling 5-on-5 play
strengths.body: Montréal takes 55% of shot attempts and 54.3% of expected goals at 5-on-5, both top-seven marks and a big step up from the sub-.480 shares of every recent season. It is broad-based: Danault, Bolduc, Hutson and Suzuki all sit near or above .585. Eight games is a small sample, but possession numbers stabilize faster than goals, and this is the strongest sign the team has improved.

strengths.title: A top-ten offense on volume
strengths.body: The Canadiens score 3.38 goals a game (9th) despite shooting a below-average 10.7%, because they generate 29.1 shots a game, 1.9 above the league. Suzuki and Hutson are carrying the creation, and Caufield's 29 shots lead the team. With shooting luck neutral or worse so far, this output looks sustainable.

strengths.title: Penalty kill holding up
strengths.body: At 82.4% the kill ranks 12th, 3.4 points above the league average, and well ahead of the sub-80% kills of most recent seasons. Some of that is small-sample noise. Even so, special teams are not where the goals against are coming from.

concerns.title: Dobes is sinking the save percentage
concerns.body: The team's .868 save % ranks 28th, and nearly all the damage sits with Jakub Dobes at .842 and -5.8 GSAx, while Fowler is at .900 and +2.2. That turns a team allowing a below-average shot count into one allowing 3.75 goals a game. Four starts each is a tiny sample, but the starts have been split evenly, and that split is the single biggest lever on this season.

concerns.title: Power play below the league
concerns.body: A 14.8% power play ranks 25th, 5.6 points under the league. Last year's unit converted at 23.1%. The personnel has the skill, and the five-on-five finishing is also running cold. A good share of this should correct, but it has cost close games.

concerns.title: Wingers and blueliners scoring against
concerns.body: Opponents' wingers are beating their usual output by 1.11 points a game (29th), and defensemen by 0.74 (28th), with defensemen taking 28.9% of the points against versus a 24.2% league share. Some of this is goaltending showing up as points allowed. Still, Dobson at -4 and Matheson at -3 over a partial season point to coverage issues on the back end as well.

trend.note: After a three-game losing streak in early October, Montréal took three of the last five, allowing 3.2 goals a game over that stretch, 0.55 below its season rate. The wins were narrow, but the defense-and-goaltending side is already tightening.

weekAhead.headline: Four games against teams that can't match Montréal's possession
weekAhead.body:
Three of the four opponents rank 23rd or worse on the site, and two of them, San Jose (.408) and Chicago (.404), are bottom-four in xGF %. That suits a team whose problem has been converting territorial edges into goals. Chicago gives up 30.3 shots a game and has a D+ crease, a spot where Montréal's volume should finally show on the scoreboard. San Jose matches Montréal's 4-3-1, but leads the league in Pts vs Goal Diff with a -0.87 goal differential behind it.

The road back half is harder. Winnipeg, 14th on the site, has a 30% power play (3rd), a B goaltending grade and one of the better defenses against centers. St. Louis shoots 13% (8th) and can punish Montréal's goaltending, but it gives up more to centers than anyone. Three straight road games after the opener is the main caveat. Anything less than a winning week would say more about the crease than the opponents.

keyMatchups.title: Shot volume against Chicago's crease
keyMatchups.body: Chicago takes only 42% of shot attempts and faces 30.3 shots a game behind a D+ goaltending group with -4.4 GSAx. Montréal already averages 29.1 shots a game. This is the likeliest game for the cold finishing to break.

keyMatchups.title: Winnipeg's power play vs Montréal's kill
keyMatchups.body: The Jets convert 30% of their chances, 3rd in the league, while being outplayed at 5-on-5 (.467 xGF %). Montréal's 82.4% kill has been steady. Staying out of the box is the best way to turn the Jets' weak even-strength play into a road win.

keyMatchups.title: Suzuki against St. Louis centers' coverage
keyMatchups.body: St. Louis allows 4.5 points a game to centers, 1.53 over expectation and dead last. Suzuki, at 21.9 minutes and 10 points, should see the minutes to exploit it. Winnipeg is the opposite case, holding centers 0.9 under expectation (4th).

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal on the road trip: whether Fowler takes the bulk of the week after Dobes' .842 start.

restOfSeason.body:
The parts of this team that tend to hold are strong: shot share, chance share and shot volume are all top-ten. The parts that tend to swing are what is dragging it down: a 96.7 PDO, a .868 save percentage and a 14.8% power play. Save percentage and power-play conversion should climb toward league norms, which would turn the goal differential positive and push Montréal back toward the playoff tier it reached last year. The one piece of luck running in their favor is the overtime record, and that should even out. It is small enough that the save-percentage correction should outweigh it.

We expect a finish around 92 to 102 points, ahead of the current 92-point pace, with goals against falling well below the current 3.75. The risk is that the goaltending problem is not noise. If neither goalie settles near .900, a strong possession team could still drift into the bubble pack in a crowded Atlantic.
swingFactors: Fowler's share of starts and whether Dobes recovers
Power-play conversion catching up to the talent
Blueline availability behind Hutson, with Matheson and Guhle having missed games

confidence.note: Eight games is thin, but the possession signal is strong and the goaltending drag is concentrated in one goalie.
